n: *Study note:* *Psalm 141*. The psalmist asks God to protect him from sin and from sinful men.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may my prayer be established [like] incense before you, the uplifting of my hands [like] an evening offering.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “door.” The Hebrew word occurs only here in the OT.

*Study note:* *My mouth…my lips*. The psalmist asks God to protect him from speaking inappropriately or sinfully.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not turn my heart toward an evil thing.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to act sinfully in practices in wickedness with men, doers of evil.”

*Study note:* *Their delicacies*. This probably refers to the enjoyment that a sinful lifestyle appears to offer.

*Translator's note:* The form יָנִי (yani) appears to be derived from the verbal root נוּא (nuʾ). Another option is to emend the form to יְנָא (yenaʾ), a Piel from נָאָה (naʾah), and translate “may choice oil not adorn my head” (see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 271). In this case, choice oil, like delicacies in v. {{Psalm 141:4|4}}, symbolize the pleasures of sin.

*Study note:* *May my head not refuse choice oil*. The psalmist compares the constructive criticism of the *godly* (see the previous line) to having refreshing olive oil poured over one’s head.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “for still, and my prayer [is] against their evil deeds.” The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult; the sequence -כִּי־עוֹד וּ (ki ʿod u-, “for still and”) occurs only here. The translation assumes an emendation to כִּי עֵד תְּפִלָּתִי (ki ʿed tefillati, “indeed a witness [is] my prayer”). The psalmist’s lament about the evil actions of sinful men (see v. {{Psalm 141:4|4}}) testifies against the wicked in the divine court.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they are thrown down by the hands of a cliff, their judges.” The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult and the meaning uncertain. The perfect verbal form is understood as rhetorical; the psalmist describes the anticipated downfall of the wicked as if it had already occurred. “Their judges” could be taken as the subject of the verb, but this makes little, if any, sense. The translation assumes the judges are the agents and that the wicked, mentioned earlier in the psalm, are the subjects of the verb.

*Translator's note:* It is unclear how this statement relates to the preceding sentence. Perhaps the judges are the referent of the pronominal subject (“they”) of the verb “will listen,” and “my words” are the referent of the pronominal subject (“they”) of the phrase “are pleasant.” The psalmist may be affirming here his confidence that he will be vindicated when he presents his case before the judges, while the wicked will be punished.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like splitting and breaking open in the earth.” The meaning of the statement and the point of the comparison are not entirely clear. Perhaps the psalmist is suggesting that he and other godly individuals are as good as dead; their bones are scattered about like dirt that is dug up and tossed aside.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my eyes [are] toward you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not lay bare my life.” Only here is the Piel form of the verb collocated with the term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “life”). In {{Isaiah 53:12|Isa 53:12}} the Lord’s servant “lays bare (the Hiphil form of the verb is used) his life to death.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the traps of the doers of evil.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is understood as a jussive of prayer. Another option is to translate, “the wicked will fall.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the same [that] I, until I pass by.” Another option is to take יַחַד (yakhad) with the preceding line, “let the wicked fall together into their own nets.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 142*. The psalmist laments his persecuted state and asks the Lord to deliver him from his enemies.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. The word is derived from a verb meaning “to be prudent; to be wise.” Various options are: “a contemplative song,” “a song imparting moral wisdom,” or “a skillful [i.e., well-written] song.” The term occurs in the superscriptions of {{Psalm 32|Pss 32}}, {{Psalm 42|42}}, {{Psalm 44|44}}, {{Psalm 45|45}}, {{Psalm 52|52-55}}, {{Psalm 74|74}}, {{Psalm 78|78}}, {{Psalm 88|88}}, {{Psalm 89|89}}, and {{Psalm 142|142}}, as well as in {{Psalm 47:7|Ps 47:7}}.

*Study note:* According to the superscription, David wrote this psalm while in “the cave.” This probably refers to either the incident recorded in {{1 Samuel 22:1|1 Sam 22:1}} or to the one recorded in {{1 Samuel 24:3|1 Sam 24:3}}. See the superscription of {{Psalm 57|Ps 57}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] my voice to the Lord I cry out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] my voice to the Lord I plead for mercy.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my trouble before him I declare.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my spirit grows faint.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you know my path.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no one who recognizes me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ a place of refuge perishes from me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no one who seeks for the sake of my life.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my portion.” The psalmist compares the Lord to landed property, which was foundational to economic stability in ancient Israel.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bring out my life.”

*Translator's note:* Or “gather around.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew idiom גָּמַל עַל (gamal ʿal) means “to repay,” here in a positive sense.
*Study note:* *Psalm 143*. As in the previous psalm, the psalmist laments his persecuted state and asks the Lord to deliver him from his enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not enter into judgment with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for no one living is innocent before you.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “an enemy.” The singular is used in a representative sense to describe a typical member of the larger group of enemies (note the plural “enemies” in vv. {{Psalm 143:9|9}}, {{Psalm 143:12|12}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he crushes on the ground my life.”

*Translator's note:* Or “sit.”

*Study note:* *Dark regions* refers to Sheol, which the psalmist views as a dark place located deep in the ground (see {{Psalm 88:6|Ps 88:6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my spirit grows faint.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in my midst my heart is shocked.” For a similar use of the Hitpolel of שָׁמֵם (shamem), see {{Isaiah 59:16|Isa 59:16}}; {{Isaiah 63:5|63:5}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “ancient times”; *Heb* “days from before.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the work of your hands.”

*Translator's note:* The words “in prayer” are supplied in the translation to clarify that the psalmist is referring to a posture of prayer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “faint” or “weary.” See {{Psalm 63:1|Ps 63:1}}.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “my soul like a faint land for you.” A verb (perhaps “thirsts”) is implied (see {{Psalm 63:1|Ps 63:1}}). The translation assumes an emendation of the preposition כ (kaf, “like”) to ב (bet, “in,” see {{Psalm 63:1|Ps 63:1}}; cf. NEB “athirst for thee in a thirsty land”). If the MT is retained, one might translate, “my soul thirsts for you, as a parched land does for water/rain” (cf. NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my spirit is failing.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not hide your face from me.” The idiom “hide the face” (1) can mean “ignore” (see {{Psalm 10:11|Pss 10:11}}; {{Psalm 13:1|13:1}}; {{Psalm 51:9|51:9}}) or (2) can carry the stronger idea of “reject” (see {{Psalm 30:7|Pss 30:7}}; {{Psalm 88:14|88:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will be equal with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the pit.” The Hebrew noun בּוֹר (bor, “pit; cistern”) is sometimes used of the grave and/or the realm of the dead. See {{Psalm 28:1|Ps 28:1}}.

*Study note:* The *morning* is sometimes viewed as the time of divine intervention (see {{Psalm 30:5|Pss 30:5}}; {{Psalm 59:16|59:16}}; {{Psalm 90:14|90:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cause me to hear in the morning your loyal love.” Here “loyal love” probably stands metonymically for an oracle of assurance promising God’s intervention as an expression of his loyal love.

*Study note:* The *way* probably refers here to God’s moral and ethical standards and requirements (see v. {{Psalm 143:10|10}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for to you I lift up my life.” The Hebrew expression נָאָשׂ נֶפֶשׁ (naʾas nefesh, “to lift up [one’s] life”) means “to desire; to long for” (see {{Deuteronomy 24:15|Deut 24:15}}; {{Proverbs 19:18|Prov 19:18}}; Jer 22:27; 44:14; Hos 4:8, as well as H. W. Wolff, *Anthropology of the Old Testament*, 16).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to you I cover,” which makes no sense. The translation assumes an emendation to נַסְתִּי (nasti, “I flee,” a Qal perfect, first singular form from נוּס, nos). Confusion of כ (kaf) and נ (nun) is attested elsewhere (see P. K. McCarter, *Textual Criticism* [GBS], 48). The collocation of נוּס (“flee”) with אֶל (ʾel, “to”) is well-attested.

*Translator's note:* Or “your will.” See {{Psalm 40:8|Ps 40:8}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your good spirit.” God’s “spirit” may refer here to his presence (see the note on the word “presence” in {{Psalm 139:7|Ps 139:7}}) or to his personal Spirit (see {{Psalm 51:10|Ps 51:10}}).

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive. Taking the statement as a prayer fits well with the petitionary tone of vv. {{Psalm 143:7|7-10a}}.

*Study note:* A *level land* (where one can walk free of obstacles) here symbolizes divine blessing and protection. See {{Psalm 26:12|Pss 26:12}} and {{Psalm 27:11|27:11}} for similar imagery.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “name,” which here stands metonymically for God’s reputation.

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal forms in vv. {{Psalm 143:11|11-12a}} are understood as expressing the psalmist’s desire. Note the petitionary tone of vv. {{Psalm 143:7|7-10a}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by your justice bring out my life from trouble.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in [or “by”] your faithfulness.”

*Translator's note:* The perfect with vav (ו) consecutive carries on the mood of the preceding imperfect.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the enemies of my life.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 144*. The psalmist expresses his confidence in God, asks for a mighty display of divine intervention in an upcoming battle, and anticipates God’s rich blessings on the nation in the aftermath of military victory.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my rocky summit.” The Lord is compared to a rocky summit where one can find protection from enemies. See {{Psalm 18:2|Ps 18:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “blessed [be] the Lord, my rocky summit.”

*Study note:* *The one who trains my hands for battle*. The psalmist attributes his skill with weapons to divine enablement (see {{Psalm 18:34|Ps 18:34}}). Egyptian reliefs picture gods teaching the king how to shoot a bow. See O. Keel, *The Symbolism of the Biblical World*, 265.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my loyal love,” which is probably an abbreviated form of “the God of my loyal love” (see {{Psalm 59:10|Ps 59:10}}, {{Psalm 59:17|17}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “my elevated place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who subdues nations beneath me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “What is mankind?” The singular noun אֱנוֹשׁ (ʾenosh) is used here in a collective sense and refers to the human race. See {{Psalm 8:5|Ps 8:5}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the son of man.” The phrase “son of man” is used here in a collective sense and refers to human beings. For other uses of the phrase in a collective or representative manner, see {{Numbers 23:19|Num 23:19}}; {{Psalm 146:3|Ps 146:3}}; {{Isaiah 51:12|Isa 51:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “take account of him.” The two imperfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 144:4|4}} describe God’s characteristic activity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “man,” or “mankind.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his days [are] like a shadow that passes away,” that is, like a late afternoon shadow made by the descending sun that will soon be swallowed up by complete darkness. See {{Psalm 102:11|Ps 102:11}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb נָטָה (natah) can carry the sense “to [cause to] bend; to [cause to] bow down.” For example, {{Genesis 49:15|Gen 49:15}} pictures Issachar as a donkey that “bends” its shoulder or back under a burden. Here the Lord causes the sky, pictured as a dome or vault, to sink down as he descends in the storm. See {{Psalm 18:9|Ps 18:9}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so you might come down.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose after the preceding imperative. The same type of construction is utilized in v. {{Psalm 144:6|6}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so they might smolder.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose after the preceding imperative.

*Study note:* *Arrows* and *lightning bolts* are associated in other texts (see {{Psalm 18:14|Pss 18:14}}; {{Psalm 77:17|77:17-18}}; Zech 9:14), as well as in ancient Near Eastern art (see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” [Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983], 187).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “stretch out your hands.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mighty waters.” The waters of the sea symbolize the psalmist’s powerful foreign enemies, as well as the realm of death they represent (see the next line and {{Psalm 18:16|Ps 18:16-17}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the hand of the sons of foreignness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who [with] their mouth speak falsehood, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” The reference to the “right hand” is probably a metonymy for an oath. When making an oath, one would raise the hand as a solemn gesture. See {{Exodus 6:8|Exod 6:8}}; {{Numbers 14:30|Num 14:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:40|Deut 32:40}}. The figure thus represents the making of false oaths (false promises).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the hand of the sons of foreignness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who [with] their mouth speak falsehood, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” See v. {{Psalm 144:8|8}} where the same expression occurs.

*Translator's note:* Some consider אֲשֶׁר (ʾasher) problematic, but here it probably indicates the anticipated consequence of the preceding request. (For other examples of אֲשֶׁר indicating purpose/result, see BDB 83 s.v. and *HALOT* 99 s.v.) If the psalmist—who appears to be a Davidic king preparing to fight a battle (see vv. {{Psalm 144:10|10-11}})—is victorious, the whole nation will be spared invasion and defeat (see v. {{Psalm 144:14|14}}) and can flourish. Some prefer to emend the form to אַשְׁרֵי (“how blessed [are our sons]”). A suffixed noun sometimes follows אַשְׁרֵי (ʾashre; see {{1 Kings 10:8|1 Kgs 10:8}}; {{Proverbs 20:7|Prov 20:7}}), but the presence of a comparative element (see “like plants”) after the suffixed noun makes the proposed reading too awkward syntactically.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “grown up in their youth.” The translation assumes that “grown up” modifies “plants” (just as “carved” modifies “corner pillars” in the second half of the verse). Another option is to take “grown up” as a predicate in relation to “our sons,” in which case one might translate, “they will be strapping youths.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun occurs only here and in Zech 9:15, where it refers to the corners of an altar.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “carved [in] the pattern of a palace.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun occurs only here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from kind to kind.” Some prefer to emend the text to מָזוֹן עַל מָזוֹן (mazon ʿal mazon, “food upon food”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they are innumerable.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in outside places.” Here the term refers to pastures and fields (see {{Job 5:10|Job 5:10}}; {{Proverbs 8:26|Prov 8:26}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “weighted down.” This probably refers (1) to the cattle having the produce from the harvest placed on their backs to be transported to the storehouses (see BDB 687 s.v. סָבַל). Other options are (2) to take this as reference to the cattle being pregnant (see *HALOT* 741 s.v. סבל pu) or (3) to their being well-fed or fattened (see L. C. Allen, *{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 288).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there [will be] no breach, and there [will be] no going out, and there [will be] no crying out in our broad places.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[O] the happiness of the people who [it is] such to them.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 145*. The psalmist praises God because he is a just and merciful king who cares for his people.

*Translator's note:* Or, hyperbolically, “forever.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and concerning his greatness there is no searching.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 145:4|4}} are understood as imperfects, indicating how the psalmist expects his audience to respond to his praise. Another option is to take the forms as jussives, indicating the psalmist’s wish, “may one generation praise…and tell about.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the splendor of the glory of your majesty, and the matters of your amazing deeds I will ponder.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is understood as an imperfect, indicating how the psalmist expects his audience to respond to his praise. Another option is to take the forms as a jussive, indicating the psalmist’s wish, “may they proclaim.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the fame of the greatness of your goodness.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 145:7|7}} are understood as imperfects, indicating how the psalmist expects his audience to respond to his praise. Another option is to take the forms as jussives, indicating the psalmist’s wish, “may they talk…and sing.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “slow to anger” (see {{Psalm 86:15|Pss 86:15}}; {{Psalm 103:8|103:8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and great of loyal love” (see {{Psalm 86:15|Pss 86:15}}; {{Psalm 103:8|103:8}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his compassion is over all his works.”

*Text-critical note:* {{Psalm 145|Psalm 145}} is an acrostic psalm, with each successive verse beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. However, in the traditional Hebrew (Masoretic) text of {{Psalm 145|Psalm 145}} there is no verse beginning with the letter nun. One would expect such a verse to appear as the fourteenth verse, between the (מ) (mem) and (ס) (samek) verses. Several ancient witnesses, including one medieval Hebrew manuscript, the Qumran scroll from cave 11, the LXX, and the Syriac, supply the missing (נ) (nun) verse, which reads as follows: “The Lord is reliable in all his words, and faithful in all his deeds.” One might paraphrase this as follows: “The Lord’s words are always reliable; his actions are always faithful.” Scholars are divided as to the originality of this verse. L. C. Allen argues for its inclusion on the basis of structural considerations (*{{Psalm 101|Psalms 101-150}}* [WBC], 294-95), but there is no apparent explanation for why, if original, it would have been accidentally omitted. The psalm may be a partial acrostic, as in {{Psalm 25|Pss 25}} and {{Psalm 34|34}} (see M. Dahood, *Psalms* [AB], 3:335). The glaring omission of the nun line would have invited a later redactor to add such a line.

*Translator's note:* Perhaps “discouraged” (see {{Psalm 57:6|Ps 57:6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the eyes of all wait for you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you give to them their food in its season” (see {{Psalm 104:27|Ps 104:27}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in all his ways.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [is] loving in all his deeds.”

*Translator's note:* In this context “desire” refers to the followers’ desire to be delivered from wicked enemies.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the desire of those who fear him, he does.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the praise of the Lord my mouth will speak.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all flesh.”
*Study note:* *Psalm 146*. The psalmist urges his audience not to trust in men, but in the Lord, the just king of the world who cares for the needy.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in a son of man, to whom there is no deliverance.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his spirit goes out, it returns to his ground; in that day his plans die.” The singular refers to the representative man mentioned in v. {{Psalm 146:3|3b}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who guards faithfulness forever.”

*Study note:* God is depicted here as a just ruler. In the ancient Near Eastern world a king was responsible for promoting justice, including caring for the weak and vulnerable, epitomized by resident foreigners, the fatherless, and widows. Cf. {{Exodus 22:21|Exod 22:21}}; Lev 19:33-34; {{Deuteronomy 10:18|Deut 10:18-19}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:14|24:14}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:17|17}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:19|27:19}}; Jer 22:3; Zech 7:10; {{Malachi 3:5|Mal 3:5}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he makes the way of the wicked twisted.” The “way of the wicked” probably refers to their course of life (see {{Proverbs 4:19|Prov 4:19}}; Jer 12:1). God makes their path tortuous in the sense that he makes them pay the harmful consequences of their actions.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for a generation and a generation.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 147*. The psalmist praises the Lord for he is the sovereign ruler of the world who cares for the needs of his covenant people.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and great of strength.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to his wisdom there is no counting.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sing to the Lord with thanksgiving.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he does not desire the strength of the horse, he does not take delight in the legs of the man.” Here “the horse” refers to the war horse used by ancient Near Eastern chariot forces, and “the man” refers to the warrior whose muscular legs epitomize his strength.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he makes your boundary peace.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “satisfies you with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who sends his word, the earth.” The Hebrew term אֶרֶץ (ʾerets, “earth”) is an adverbial accusative; one must supply a preposition before it (such as “through” or “to”) in the English translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “swiftly his word runs.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who gives snow like wool, frost like ashes he scatters.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his ice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Before his cold, who can stand?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he sends his word and melts them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he blows his breath.”
*Study note:* *Psalm 148*. The psalmist calls upon all creation to praise the Lord, for he is the creator and sovereign king of the world.

*Translator's note:* Or “heavenly messengers.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all his host.”

*Study note:* The “water” mentioned here corresponds to the “waters above” mentioned in {{Genesis 1:7|Gen 1:7}}. See also {{Psalm 104:3|Ps 104:3}}. For a discussion of the picture envisioned by the psalmist, see L. I. J. Stadelmann, *The Hebrew Conception of the World*, 47.

*Translator's note:* Or “forever and ever.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it will not pass away.”

*Translator's note:* In {{Psalm 119:83|Ps 119:83}} the noun refers to “smoke,” but here, where the elements of nature are addressed, the clouds, which resemble smoke, are probably in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[that] does his word.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he lifted up a horn for his people.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (see {{Deuteronomy 33:17|Deut 33:17}}; {{1 Kings 22:11|1 Kgs 22:11}}; {{Psalm 92:10|Ps 92:10}}). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Sam 2:10}}; {{Psalm 75:10|Pss 75:10}}; {{Psalm 89:17|89:17}}, {{Psalm 89:24|24}}; {{Psalm 92:10|92:10}}; Lam 2:17). Another option is to take the “horn” as a symbol for the Davidic king, through whom the Lord gives his people military victory.

*Translator's note:* “[there is] praise for all his loyal followers, to the sons of Israel, the people near him.” Here “praise” stands by metonymy for the victory that prompts it.

*Study note:* *Psalm 149*. The psalmist calls upon God’s people to praise him because he is just and avenges them.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his praise in the assembly of the godly ones.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sons.”

*Study note:* The Lord is the *King* here, as the parallelism in the previous line (“their creator”) indicates.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in glory.” Here “glory” probably refers to the “honor” that belongs to the Lord’s people as a result of their deliverance (see v. {{Psalm 149:4|4}}).

*Translator's note:* The significance of the reference to “beds” is unclear. Perhaps the point is that they should rejoice at all times, even when falling asleep or awaking.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they”; the referent (the enemies of the people of God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to do against them judgment [that] is written.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it is honor for all his godly ones.” The judgment of the oppressive kings will bring vindication and honor to God’s people (see vv. {{Psalm 149:4|4-5}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 150*. The Psalter concludes with a resounding call for praise from everything that has breath.
